courses.title: General Chemistry (CHM 101/102)
courses.description: Atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, acids and bases, and an introduction to organic chemistry for 100 Level health science students.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
topics.summary: Subatomic particles, isotopes, electronic configuration and periodic trends.

material.heading: The atom
material.body: An atom has a nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral) surrounded by electrons (negative). The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons; the mass number (A) is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons (e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14; iodine-131 is used in thyroid therapy). Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy (Aufbau principle): 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d …; each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin (Pauli exclusion principle) and electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly first (Hund's rule).

material.heading: Periodic trends
material.body: Across a period (left to right) atomic radius decreases while ionisation energy and electronegativity increase, because nuclear charge increases with electrons added to the same shell. Down a group, atomic radius increases and ionisation energy decreases because of extra shells and shielding. Group 1 are alkali metals, group 17 halogens, group 18 noble gases. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.
keyPoints: Across a period: radius ↓, ionisation energy ↑, electronegativity ↑
Down a group: radius ↑, ionisation energy ↓

questions.stem: The atomic number of an element is the number of:
questions.explanation: Atomic number (Z) equals the number of protons in the nucleus.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same Z but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.stem: The electronic configuration of sodium (Z = 11) is:
questions.explanation: Sodium has 11 electrons: 2, 8, 1.

questions.stem: Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.explanation: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0 on the Pauling scale).

questions.stem: Moving down Group 1 of the periodic table, atomic radius:
questions.explanation: Extra electron shells make atoms larger down a group.

questions.stem: No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers. This is:
questions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle limits an orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

questions.stem: An atom with 17 protons and 18 neutrons has a mass number of:
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 35 (chlorine-35).

questions.stem: Group 18 elements are known as:
questions.explanation: Group 18 elements (He, Ne, Ar…) are the noble gases.

topics.title: Chemical Bonding and Intermolecular Forces
topics.summary: Ionic, covalent, coordinate and metallic bonds, molecular shapes and hydrogen bonding.

material.heading: Types of bonds
material.body: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer between metals and non-metals (e.g. NaCl) and give high-melting solids that conduct when molten or dissolved. Covalent bonds form by sharing electron pairs between non-metals (e.g. H2O, CH4). A coordinate (dative) bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons come from one atom (e.g. NH4+, H3O+). Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.
keyPoints: Dative bond: both electrons from one atom (NH4+)

material.heading: Shapes and intermolecular forces
material.body: VSEPR theory predicts shape from electron pairs: CH4 is tetrahedral (109.5°), NH3 trigonal pyramidal (~107°), H2O bent (~104.5°), CO2 linear (180°). Intermolecular forces, in increasing strength, are London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonding (H bonded to N, O or F) explains water's high boiling point and holds DNA base pairs and protein secondary structures together.
keyPoints: Hydrogen bonds: H attached to N, O or F
H-bonds explain water's high boiling point

questions.stem: The bond in sodium chloride is:
questions.explanation: Na transfers an electron to Cl, forming Na+ and Cl− ions.

questions.stem: The ammonium ion (NH4+) contains a:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H+, forming a dative bond.

questions.stem: The shape of the water molecule is:
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen give water a bent shape (~104.5°).

questions.stem: The bond angle in methane is about:
questions.explanation: Methane is tetrahedral with bond angles of 109.5°.

questions.stem: Water's unusually high boiling point is due to:
questions.explanation: Extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules raises its boiling point.

questions.stem: The weakest intermolecular force is the:
questions.explanation: London (dispersion) forces are the weakest intermolecular attractions.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is a linear molecule with a bond angle of:
questions.explanation: CO2 is linear, O=C=O at 180°.

questions.stem: Base pairs in DNA are held together by:
questions.explanation: A–T pairs form two and G–C pairs three hydrogen bonds.

topics.title: The Mole and Stoichiometry
topics.summary: Moles, molar mass, concentration, empirical formulae and balancing equations.

material.heading: The mole
material.body: One mole contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). Number of moles = mass ÷ molar mass. Molar mass is the relative formula mass in g/mol (e.g. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol). At standard temperature and pressure, one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³. The empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it (e.g. glucose C6H12O6 has empirical formula CH2O).

material.heading: Solutions and concentration
material.body: Molarity (mol/dm³) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in dm³. Dilution follows C1V1 = C2V2. Percentage w/v is grams per 100 mL: normal saline is 0.9% w/v NaCl (0.9 g in 100 mL, about 154 mmol/L). In balancing equations, the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides; coefficients give mole ratios for calculations.

questions.explanation: One mole contains 6.02 × 10^23 particles.

questions.explanation: Dividing by 6 gives CH2O.

questions.explanation: H2 : H2O is 2 : 2 (1:1), so 4 mol H2 gives 4 mol H2O.

topics.title: Acids, Bases, pH and Buffers
topics.summary: Acid–base theories, pH calculations, neutralisation and buffer solutions in the body.

material.heading: Acids, bases and pH
material.body: Arrhenius acids release H+ in water; Brønsted–Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors; Lewis acids accept electron pairs. pH = −log10[H+]. At 25 °C neutral water has pH 7; acids have pH below 7 and bases above 7. A change of one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H+]. Strong acids (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3) ionise completely; weak acids (ethanoic acid, carbonic acid) only partially.

material.heading: Buffers
material.body: A buffer resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its salt). The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]). The bicarbonate buffer (H2CO3/HCO3−) is the main extracellular buffer keeping blood pH at 7.35–7.45; haemoglobin, phosphate and protein buffers also contribute.

questions.stem: A solution has [H+] = 1 × 10^−3 mol/dm³. Its pH is:
According to Brønsted–Lowry, a base is a:
questions.explanation: Brønsted–Lowry bases accept protons.

questions.stem: Normal arterial blood pH is:
questions.explanation: Blood pH is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45.

questions.stem: The main extracellular buffer in blood is the:
questions.explanation: The carbonic acid/bicarbonate system is the chief extracellular buffer.

questions.stem: Which is a strong acid?
questions.explanation: HCl ionises completely in water.

questions.stem: When [A−] = [HA] in a buffer, the pH equals:
questions.explanation: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: Solution X has pH 4 and Y has pH 6. Compared with Y, X has:
questions.explanation: Two pH units = 10² = 100-fold difference.

questions.stem: A buffer is best made from:
options: A strong acid and a strong base
A strong acid and its salt
A weak acid and its salt (conjugate base)
questions.explanation: A weak acid with its conjugate base resists pH change.

topics.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
topics.summary: Hydrocarbons, functional groups, isomerism and IUPAC naming.

material.heading: Hydrocarbons and naming
material.body: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated with single bonds; alkenes (CnH2n) have a C=C double bond and undergo addition reactions (e.g. decolourising bromine water); alkynes (CnH2n−2) have a triple bond. IUPAC names use the longest carbon chain (meth-1, eth-2, prop-3, but-4, pent-5, hex-6 carbons) with suffixes for the functional group. Benzene (C6H6) is aromatic with delocalised π electrons and undergoes substitution rather than addition.
keyPoints: Alkanes CnH2n+2; alkenes CnH2n; alkynes CnH2n−2

material.heading: Functional groups and isomerism
material.body: Important functional groups are alcohols (–OH, e.g. ethanol), aldehydes (–CHO), ketones (C=O within a chain, e.g. propanone/acetone), carboxylic acids (–COOH), esters (–COO–), amines (–NH2) and amides (–CONH2). Isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements: structural isomers differ in bonding sequence; stereoisomers include geometric (cis/trans) isomers and optical isomers (enantiomers), which arise from a chiral carbon bonded to four different groups. Drug enantiomers may differ in activity (e.g. thalidomide).
keyPoints: Enantiomers can have different drug effects

questions.stem: The general formula of the alkanes is:
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, CnH2n+2.

questions.stem: Which compound decolourises bromine water?
questions.explanation: Alkenes such as ethene undergo addition with bromine.

questions.stem: The functional group of a carboxylic acid is:
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids contain –COOH.

questions.stem: Propanone (acetone) belongs to the class of:
questions.explanation: Propanone has a C=O within the carbon chain, making it a ketone.

questions.stem: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is described as:
questions.explanation: Such a carbon is a stereocentre that gives rise to enantiomers.

questions.stem: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are:
questions.explanation: Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in arrangement.

questions.stem: The IUPAC name for CH3CH2CH2CH3 is:
questions.explanation: Four carbons with single bonds: butane.

questions.stem: Benzene typically undergoes:
questions.explanation: Aromatic stability makes substitution favoured over addition.
